items.title: Start here: an ERP data model and its security findings
items.body:
IDURAR is an open-source ERP/CRM for clients, invoices and payments: Express and Mongoose in `idurar-erp-crm/backend/`, React in `idurar-erp-crm/frontend/`. This quest studies it the way a reviewer joining the team would: what the data model promises, and where the code does not keep those promises.

Read these three guides from `fable docs/`, in order:

1. `03-architecture-and-patterns/02-data-model-and-persistence.md`: entities, embedding versus referencing, the cached balance, transactions, indexes and schema changes.
2. `03-architecture-and-patterns/03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md`: the validation layers, authentication versus authorization, password handling.
3. `05-quality-engineering/05-security-checklist.md`: a threat map with findings marked *confirmed* or *investigate*.

Every finding cites a file and line. Open each one and decide for yourself whether it holds at this commit; a guide can overstate a finding, and the code is what runs. Several file names repeat (`paginatedList.js`, `update.js`, `read.js` exist per controller), so check the full path before you trust a line number.

excerpts.quote: The security surfaces of IDURAR mapped to real code, then a pre-merge checklist.

readMore.why: The architecture module this quest draws on.

items.title: A unique index enforces what code cannot
items.body:
Invoice numbers are allocated by the application, so two concurrent creates can pick the same `number`. A unique compound index on `{ number: 1, year: 1 }` makes MongoDB reject the second insert, which closes the race at the database no matter what the code does. The guide marks it as one of the two safe bets.

- *Unique on client alone*: that would allow only one invoice per client.
- *`{ removed: 1, enabled: -1 }`*: the guide lists it for the default sort; it is not unique and enforces nothing.
- *TTL on date*: a TTL index deletes documents after a time; it would destroy invoices, not prevent duplicates.

readMore.why: The number and year fields with no index.

items.title: Objects are rejected where a value is expected
items.body:
With Express 4's default query parser, `equal[$ne]=` arrives as the object `{ $ne: ... }`. The generic `paginatedList` checks `typeof equal === 'object'` and returns `400` with "Invalid filter value" before building any query. Only a primitive `equal` becomes `{ [filter]: equal }`. This is the guide's "query guard" layer.

- *Runs the query with $ne*: that is the attack the guard exists to stop.
- *Casts to a string*: no cast happens; the request is rejected.
- *Drops equal*: the code returns early; it does not fall back to an unfiltered list.

readMore.why: The threat map row for NoSQL injection.

items.title: Atomic credit, stale status
items.body:
Both requests read the invoice first (`credit` 0) and pass the overpay guard. Each then runs `$inc: { credit: 50 }`, which is atomic, so credit ends at 100: no increment is lost, as the guide says. But each computes `paymentStatus` in JavaScript from the credit it read: 100 is not equal to 0 + 50, and 0 + 50 > 0, so both `$set: { paymentStatus: 'partially' }`. The invoice is fully paid but marked partially.

- *credit 50*: `$inc` is applied by the server atomically, so neither increment overwrites the other.
- *credit 100 and paid*: correct credit, but status comes from the stale read, not from the new credit.
- *credit 50 and paid*: no request ever computes paid here.

readMore.why: The guide on $inc and concurrent payments.

items.title: Concept: a cached balance kept by several writes
items.body:
An invoice stores `credit` (money paid so far) and `paymentStatus` on itself instead of summing its payments on every read. That is **denormalization**: faster reads, in exchange for keeping the copy correct on every write that affects it.

Two separate questions decide whether such a copy stays correct:

- **Crashes.** If one logical change takes several writes, what is left when the process stops halfway? Look up what MongoDB requires before a multi-document transaction can be used, and compare it with how IDURAR runs in development.
- **Concurrency.** If two requests change the same invoice at once, can one overwrite the other? Read `backend/src/controllers/appControllers/paymentController/create.js` and, for each field it writes to the invoice, note how its new value is produced and from which data.

Then read the **Indexes** and **How to safely change the schema** sections of the data-model guide. For each proposed index, ask what query it serves and whether it would also enforce a rule.

excerpts.quote: is a cached running total of payments

readMore.why: The payment controller that maintains the cached balance.

items.title: Embed what is owned, reference what stands alone
items.body:
Line items are part of an invoice: no identity outside it, always read with it, never queried across invoices. The guide calls this "embed when owned and bounded", so `Invoice.items` is an embedded array. Payments are created, edited, deleted and listed on their own, so they are a collection, and `Invoice.payment` keeps an array of refs to them.

- *A unique index on itemName*: no index is declared on items; embedding is about ownership, not indexing.
- *Payments embedded in the client*: `Payment` is its own model with `client` and `invoice` refs.
- *Mongoose cannot reference subdocuments*: the choice is a modeling decision; Mongoose supports refs from any schema path.

excerpts.quote: This is the "embed when owned and bounded" rule.

readMore.why: The Invoice schema with embedded items and payment refs.

items.title: loggedSessions only shrinks on logout
items.body:
Each successful login runs `$push: { loggedSessions: token }` (password reset pushes too). The only code that removes entries is `logout.js`: it `$pull`s the presented token, or clears the array when no token is sent. A user who never logs out leaves every old token in the array, expired or not, so it grows without bound.

- *A nightly job*: no scheduled job exists in the backend.
- *isValidAuthToken pulls expired tokens*: it only reads `loggedSessions`; it never writes it.
- *A TTL index*: TTL indexes expire whole documents by a date field, not array elements, and none is declared.

readMore.why: The unbounded-growth row of the threat map.

items.title: Authenticated is not authorized
items.body:
The request passes `isValidAuthToken`, so A is authenticated. The generic `read.js` then runs `Model.findOne({ _id: req.params.id, removed: false })`. Nothing compares the record's `createdBy` with `req.admin`, so A receives B's client. With one owner this is by design; with two users it is an IDOR (insecure direct object reference).

- *403 on createdBy*: no controller checks `createdBy`; it is stamped for attribution only.
- *404 scoped to the caller*: the filter has no caller condition.
- *401 for another owner's token*: A's token is A's own and valid; whose record it is never enters authentication.

excerpts.quote: const result = await Model.findOne({ _id: req.params.id, removed: false, }).exec();

readMore.why: Why missing authorization is fine today and critical with a second user.

items.title: The generic update resets removed
items.body:
The first statement of `createCRUDController/update.js` is `req.body.removed = false;`, and only then is `req.body` passed as the update to `findOneAndUpdate`. So the new name is saved and `removed` is written as false. The mass-assignment finding is real for other fields (`createdBy`, `enabled`, any schema path), but the security checklist's claim that a client "could set `removed`" does not hold at this commit.

- *Soft-deletes the client*: the override runs before the update, so removed stays false.
- *400 for a disallowed field*: there is no whitelist or Joi check on generic updates.
- *Ignores the whole body*: every other body field is applied.

readMore.why: The mass-assignment finding this question tests.

items.title: Soft-deleted invoices stay downloadable
items.body:
`downloadPdf` derives the model from the directory and runs `Model.findOne({ _id: id })`. Unlike the CRUD controllers it has no `removed: false` condition, so a soft-deleted invoice is still found and its PDF generated and served. The route is also outside the authenticated mounts.

- *404 for removed*: only a missing document triggers the not-found path; removed ones are found.
- *401 without a session*: `/download` has no auth middleware.
- *410 Gone*: the handler never uses 410.

readMore.why: The guide on the download route and soft delete.

items.title: bcrypt already salts
items.body:
bcrypt creates a random salt for every hash and stores it inside the hash string. IDURAR also prepends its own random `shortid` and stores it in the same `AdminPassword` document. Since it sits next to the hash, it is not a secret, and bcrypt's own salt already defeats precomputed tables, so the guide calls it a talking point that adds little, not a vulnerability.

- *Main defence, bcrypt stores no salt*: bcrypt embeds its salt in the hash.
- *A pepper kept elsewhere*: the shortid is stored in the database beside the hash.
- *Speed*: the bcrypt cost factor sets the work; prepending a string does not change it.

items.title: The download router has no auth
items.body:
`app.js` mounts `coreAuthRouter` on `/api` (login and reset), then `coreApiRouter` and `erpApiRouter` on `/api` behind `adminAuth.isValidAuthToken`, then `app.use('/download', coreDownloadRouter)` with no middleware at all. That router serves the generated invoice and payment PDFs, so anyone holding a URL can fetch one.

- *erpApiRouter*: mounted with `isValidAuthToken` first.
- *coreApiRouter*: also mounted with `isValidAuthToken` first.
- *The invoice routes of erpApiRouter*: they live inside a protected router, so they inherit its auth.

items.title: Transactions need a replica set
items.body:
MongoDB multi-document transactions run only on a replica set or a sharded cluster. A single standalone `mongod`, the default local setup for IDURAR, rejects `startTransaction`. So the fix for the crash window ("wrap the payment insert and invoice update in `withTransaction`") first needs a deployment change, which the guide calls the crux of the interview answer.

- *WiredTiger without journaling*: transactions need WiredTiger, but turning the journal off is not a requirement and weakens durability.
- *A sharded cluster with three shards*: sharding is one option, not a requirement; a replica set is enough.
- *Autopopulate everywhere*: that plugin only populates refs; it has nothing to do with transactions.

excerpts.quote: but **only on a replica set**, which the default single-node dev setup isn

items.title: Concept: who may do what, and which input is trusted
items.body:
*Authentication* asks who you are; *authorization* asks what you may do. A system can be strict about the first and silent about the second.

Map both in IDURAR:

- In `backend/src/app.js`, list every `app.use` mount and the middleware in front of it.
- In `backend/src/controllers/middlewaresControllers/createCRUDController/`, read `read.js`, `paginatedList.js` and `update.js` in full. For each, write down the exact query filter it builds and which request fields reach the database unchanged.
- Read `backend/src/handlers/downloadHandler/downloadPdf.js` and compare its lookup filter with the CRUD ones.

For input handling, the validation guide lists a *query guard*. Find it, and note what kind of value it rejects and how.

Finally, `authUser.js` and `logout.js` in `createAuthMiddleware/` both write to the same array. List every place in the backend that writes to it.

excerpts.quote: These are different and the distinction is a top interview topic.

readMore.why: The threat map and pre-merge checklist.

items.title: Add, backfill, then require
items.body:
MongoDB stores no schema, so existing invoices simply lack `notes`. If the Mongoose schema made it `required` at once, every old invoice would fail validation the next time it is saved. The guide's order is: deploy it as optional, backfill the existing documents, then tighten it to `required` in a later deploy.

- *MongoDB rejects old documents*: MongoDB itself enforces no schema here; only Mongoose validates, and only on save.
- *Required with a default rewrites documents*: a default fills the value in memory; stored documents change only when each is saved.
- *Rename first*: renaming is a different, riskier change and does not populate old documents.

excerpts.quote: add as optional → backfill existing docs → tighten to `required` in a later deploy

readMore.why: The four kinds of schema change.
